docs.title: GameStart
docs.text:
Welcome! GameStart is a cozy first-person tidy-up game set in a late-90s/2000s video-game store. You're the overnight clerk: the whole shop starts out in a glorious mess, and box by box you put it back in order — game boxes on the right shelves, consoles on their stands, merch where merch belongs. No timers, no customers, no pressure. Just you, the hum of the CRT at the counter, and a store that slowly becomes yours.

The twist: if you choose to connect your Steam profile, the games on the shelves are your own library — your actual games appear as physical boxes you can pick up, flip over, and shelve. (Totally optional — there's a built-in fictional catalog too. See Privacy.)

Heads up: GameStart is in development and not yet released. This wiki describes the current development build. Anything marked Planned is design intent and may change before release.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is the game out? Not yet — GameStart is in development. This wiki tracks the development build; pages mark in-development features as Planned.

What platforms? PC first (the game is built and tested for desktop). Anything beyond that is unannounced.

Do I need a Steam account to play? No. Connecting your Steam profile is optional — without it you get a full store of original fictional games. See Privacy.

Does my Steam data get uploaded anywhere? No. It's fetched from your public profile onto your machine and stays there. Privacy has the full breakdown.

Is there co-op? Planned — tidying the store with a friend is on the roadmap, but it's not in the current build.

Is there a timer or fail state? No. No customers, no shifts to survive, no clock pressure — time of day is ambiance. The store only ever gets tidier.

Can I rebind controls? Yes, fully — keyboard/mouse and gamepad. See Getting Started for defaults.

I get motion sick in first-person games. A field-of-view slider is planned. Camera comfort options are a stated design goal.

Can I mod it? Yes — content packs can restock the store with custom fictional games, managed from an in-game screen. See Modding.

The last box — will I be hunting one lost item forever? The design explicitly guards against the "399 of 400" problem: the planned robot buddy gadget specializes in recovering lost items, and progress cues mark what's left.

docs.title: Controls (keyboard & mouse)
docs.text:
Every control can be rebound in the settings — this is the default layout.

Action Default Move W A S D Look Mouse Pick up / interact E or Left Click Put down / throw Right Click (hold to throw harder) Drop Q Cycle through what you're holding Scroll wheel, or tap R Cart menu R Face a shelf (neaten a row) F Inspect the held box (look closer) Hold V Store map Tab Jump Space Sprint Left Shift Crouch Left Ctrl Tool shortcuts 1 – 5 Pause Esc

Gamepad is supported with equivalent bindings.

docs.title: Your first night
docs.text:
1. Look around. The store opens in "arranged chaos" — games and merch piled on counters, fixtures, and the floor. Everything loose has a home somewhere.
  2. Pick things up (E / Left Click). You can carry a small stack at once — the counter in the corner of your screen shows which item is "in hand" (like 2 / 5); scroll to flip through the stack.
  3. Find the right spot. Hold a box near a shelf and a ghost preview shows where it would land. Matching games glow to help you spot where the rest of the stack lives.
  4. Place it. If the spot is right, you get a satisfying chime and XP. If the box is in the wrong section, the shelf's price tag turns red — see Tidying & Price Tags.
  5. Check the terminal. The CRT computer at the counter is the store's brain: look up any game, see your play stats, and browse store info.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: The game autosaves when you pause. One store, one continuous save — progress you make stays made.

docs.title: Modding
docs.text:
GameStart's store stock is data-driven, and the game has a built-in, player-visible modding surface: packs.

Pre-release note: the pack format is still evolving. Packs you make today may need updates as the game develops.

docs.title: Packs
docs.text:
A pack is a folder of content that changes what fills the store — the fictional games on the shelves: their titles, platforms, box styles, and cover art.

In the game's pack screen you can:

  • See every installed pack (it says "No packs installed" until you add one).
  • Enable/disable each pack with its toggle.
  • See each pack's load order (#1, #2, …) — later packs win when two packs touch the same game.
  • Click "Open packs folder" to jump straight to where packs live on disk.

docs.title: Installing a pack
docs.text:
1. In the game, open the pack screen and click "Open packs folder".
  2. Drop the pack's folder in there (one folder per pack).
  3. Back in the game, enable it with its toggle.

docs.title: Making a pack
docs.text:
The honest answer for now: the format is documented for developers rather than polished for creators — it's a folder of plain-text files describing games plus image files for cover art. If you're comfortable poking at files, see the Dev Glossary for where the technical documentation lives.

Planned: first-class mod support with Steam Workshop sharing, so packs can be subscribed to instead of hand-copied.

docs.title: What packs can't touch
docs.text: Packs change the fictional catalog. Your connected Steam library (if you opted in) is your own data and isn't overridden by packs — see Privacy.

docs.title: Privacy — the optional Steam connection
docs.text: GameStart can put your own Steam library on the store's shelves. This page is the plain-English record of exactly what that means. The short version: it's opt-in, it's read-only, and nothing about your library ever leaves your machine.

docs.title: What happens if you opt in
docs.text:
• You provide your public Steam profile (no password, no login through the game — it reads the same public info anyone can see on your profile page).
  • The game fetches your owned games list, playtime, and cover art, live, onto your machine.
  • That data is used to fill the shelves, print the boxes, and (in the planned quiz fixtures) generate quizzes about your play history.
  • Cover art is cached locally so later sessions load faster.

docs.title: What never happens
docs.text:
• Your library data is never uploaded anywhere or shared with anyone. It travels one way: from Steam to your machine.
  • Nothing from your library is bundled into the game — every player's store is fetched fresh from their own profile.
  • The game never asks for your Steam password or acts on your account.

docs.title: If you opt out (or your profile is private)
docs.text: You get the fictional catalog — a full store of original parody games with authored stats. Everything works, including the planned quizzes (they just quiz the fictional catalog instead of your backlog). You can change your mind either way at any time; the store restocks accordingly.

docs.title: Store Guide
docs.text: Your store is one big room with distinct sections. Learning the layout is the game — the better you know it, the faster every box finds its home. Press Tab for the store map anytime.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• New Releases wall — the latest games, shiny boxes with a new-release badge.
  • Pre-Owned wall — used copies, marked with the classic pre-owned sticker.
  • Platform shelves — each console family has its own shelving run; the box shape gives it away (chunky cartridge boxes, slim jewel cases, tall keepcases, PC big boxes, little disc cases…). Colored section signs overhead mark each zone.
  • The counter — the heart of the store: the register area and the terminal, a CRT computer where you can look up any game in the store and (if you connected Steam) your own play history.
  • Glass cases & pegboards — some items live in locked glass cases or hang on pegs rather than sitting on shelves.

docs.title: Reading a game box
docs.text:
The box itself tells you a lot:

  • Front: cover art, platform styling, title.
  • Back: release year, publisher blurb, and a "staff pick"-style badge that hints how much that game has been played. Hold V to inspect a box up close.
  • Fine details (exact hours played, last played) aren't on the box — those live in the terminal.

docs.title: Section signs & plaques
docs.text: Each section has an overhead sign. Planned: when a section is completely tidied, its sign lights up and stays lit — the store itself becomes your progress bar, ending in a grand opening when everything is done.

docs.title: Quiz walls — Planned
docs.text:
Two special fixtures are planned that quiz you on your own library:

  • Wall of Shame — arrange your owned-but-barely-played games in order. Yes, it knows.
  • Hall of Honor — your most-played games, ranked.

You place boxes into the fixture's slots in what you believe is the right order. Getting it right earns talent points (Talents & Gear). Price tags never appear on these fixtures — that would leak the answers. If you haven't connected Steam, the quizzes use the fictional catalog instead.

docs.title: Talents & Gear
docs.text: Most of this page is Planned — it describes the in-development "finite night" update. The current build has XP, levels, and a money counter; the update replaces money with talents.

docs.title: Talent points — Planned
docs.text:
One currency: talent points. You earn them two ways:

  • Quizzes (the fast lane): complete a quiz fixture correctly — like the Wall of Shame or Hall of Honor — and get paid in talents.
  • Sorting (the slow trickle): regular tidying XP slowly converts into talent points on its own.

Spend talents to unlock gear and upgrades. The carrying-capacity cart upgrade (money- bought in the current build) becomes a talent unlock.

docs.title: The gadget shelf — Planned
docs.text:
Four store gadgets, each a loving parody of infamous game-industry hardware. Final names are still being decided, so for now, by function:

Gadget What it does The power glove (parody) Magnet grab — yank matching loose strays to your hand from across the aisle The red visor (parody) Scanner vision — highlights where your held box belongs, and lights up matching strays The robot buddy (parody) A little helper that fetches lost items — and, at its top tier, may even shelve for you The pocket terminal (parody) The counter terminal's database, portable — check play stats right at the shelf. The quiz-solver's best friend

A note for quiz fans: early quiz fixtures are designed to be solvable bare-handed — gear makes them comfortable, never required.

One current-build freebie is moving: the glow that highlights matching games while you hold a box will become part of the red visor's basic tier in the update.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
Pick up → find the right spot → place → watch the store come together. Every copy of a game has a proper home: the right section, the right shelf, the right row. When you hold a box near shelving, a ghost preview shows exactly where it would sit, and other copies of the same game glow so you can reunite the stack.

Neaten a row anytime with Face (F) — pulling boxes forward into a tidy front line, just like real shelf work.

docs.title: Price tags: white good, red bad
docs.text:
Every row of games on a shelf has a price tag on the rail under it.

  • White tag — that run of boxes is where it belongs. All is well.
  • Red tag — something in that run is in the wrong section. Fix the placement and the tag turns white again, instantly.

If you place a box in a spot that fits but is the wrong section, the tag goes red on the spot — that's the store telling you "close, but no." No penalty, no timer; it just stays red until you make it right.

docs.title: Finishing a game (all copies home)
docs.text: Planned: when the last copy of a game is correctly shelved, that stack gets a persistent gleam — a little "done ✓" the store remembers. Finish every game in a section and the section's overhead sign lights up. Light every section and the store holds its grand opening — roll credits. The current build tracks your tidying progress; the persistent gleams, lit plaques, and finale are being built as part of the finite-night update.

docs.title: XP
docs.text: Correct placements earn XP (you'll see the +XP pop). XP raises your clerk level. In the current build there's also a money counter used for a cart upgrade — the in-development update replaces money entirely with talent points (Talents & Gear).
